questions.q: Under the electron microscope, rabies virus is seen to have a shape described as:
questions.x: Rabies virus is an enveloped helical RNA virus with a characteristic bullet shape. Poxviruses are brick-shaped and bacteriophages are tadpole-like.

questions.q: A child has high fever, cough, red eyes and a red rash spreading over the body. The disease is caught by breathing in droplets. The most likely viral disease is:
questions.x: Measles spreads through respiratory droplets and causes fever, cough and a typical red skin rash. Polio causes paralysis, rabies attacks nerves after a bite, and hepatitis A affects the liver.

questions.q: Which of the following viruses has a polyhedral (icosahedral) capsid?
questions.x: Adenovirus has a regular icosahedral capsid. Tobacco mosaic virus is helical, T4 is complex (head plus tail) and rabies virus is bullet-shaped.

questions.q: Removing the amino group from aspartate leaves a four-carbon acid that is fed straight into the citric acid cycle. This acid is:
questions.x: The carbon skeleton of aspartate is oxaloacetate, the four-carbon acid of the Krebs cycle. Different amino acids enter at different points of the pathway.

questions.q: After deamination of an amino acid, the remaining carbon skeleton is a:
questions.x: Removing the amino group leaves an organic keto acid. This carbon skeleton can then enter respiration as pyruvate, acetyl CoA or a Krebs cycle intermediate.

questions.q: The two DNA strands are held together by many hydrogen bonds, each of which is weak. The advantage of this is that:
o: The strands can be separated for copying, yet the molecule is stable overall
The two strands can never be separated
Bases can easily move from one strand to the other
The backbone breaks easily when the cell divides
questions.x: Each hydrogen bond is easy to break, so the strands can be unzipped for replication and transcription. Together, thousands of them keep the double helix stable.

questions.q: A base substitution changes the codon UAC (for tyrosine) to UAA. The most likely result is:
o: A shorter polypeptide, because translation stops at this point
One amino acid replaced by a different one
No change, because the code is degenerate
A longer polypeptide, because a stop codon is lost
questions.x: UAA is a stop codon, so the ribosome stops early and releases an incomplete, shorter polypeptide. Here no amino acid is substituted, since none is coded.

questions.q: In the term 'acylglycerol', the word 'acyl' refers to:
o: A phosphate group joined to glycerol
A sugar residue joined to glycerol
A free hydroxyl group of glycerol
A fatty acid residue joined to glycerol by an ester bond
questions.x: An acyl group (R–CO–) is what remains of a fatty acid after it forms an ester bond with an alcohol. Acylglycerols are therefore glycerol esters of fatty acids.

questions.q: The molecular formula of glycerol is:
questions.x: Glycerol is propane-1,2,3-triol, CH2OH–CHOH–CH2OH, which is C3H8O3. C3H6O3 is the formula of lactic acid and glyceraldehyde, and C6H12O6 is a hexose.

questions.q: In which reaction does water act as a reagent so that energy is released for cell work?
o: Condensation of amino acids into a protein
Hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and phosphate
Synthesis of fat from glycerol and fatty acids
questions.x: ATP + H₂O → ADP + phosphate releases energy that the cell uses. The other three reactions are condensations that release water and need energy.

questions.q: Which pair of compounds are both organic?
questions.x: Urea and glycerol both have carbon bonded to hydrogen, so both are organic. Carbon dioxide, water and sodium chloride are inorganic.

questions.q: An enzyme stops working after being heated to 70 °C, even after it is cooled again. The main reason is that:
o: Its peptide bonds have all been broken
It has been converted into a carbohydrate
Its amino acids have changed into different amino acids
Its three-dimensional shape, including the active site, has been changed
questions.x: Heat breaks the weak bonds that hold the folded shape, so the active site no longer fits its substrate. The peptide bonds and amino acid sequence stay the same.

questions.q: Casein in milk and albumin in egg white mainly serve as:
questions.x: Casein and egg albumin store amino acids that nourish the young animal or embryo. Structural proteins include keratin and collagen; contractile proteins include actin and myosin.

questions.q: In eukaryotic cells, most genes are located on the:
questions.x: Genes are segments of DNA, and almost all of a eukaryotic cell's DNA is in the chromosomes of the nucleus. Ribosomes read genes' messages but do not carry genes.

questions.q: Essential amino acids are those that:
o: Cannot be made by the body and must be taken in the diet
Are found only in plant proteins
Contain sulphur in their R groups
questions.x: The body can make some amino acids, but essential ones must come from food. They are found in both animal and plant proteins and are needed throughout life.

questions.q: Inside a cell, peptide bonds are formed on the:
questions.x: Ribosomes are the sites of protein synthesis, where amino acids are joined by peptide bonds. Lysosomes digest materials, and the Golgi apparatus modifies and packages proteins.

questions.q: The enzyme-controlled reactions that build complex molecules from simpler ones are together called:
questions.x: Anabolism is the building part of metabolism, such as making proteins from amino acids. Catabolism and hydrolysis break molecules down; denaturation is loss of a protein's shape.

questions.q: Mature red blood cells of mammals have no nucleus. As a result, they:
o: Carry less haemoglobin than other cells
Can divide faster than other cells
Are able to carry out aerobic respiration better
Cannot divide or make new proteins
questions.x: Without a nucleus a cell has no genes to direct protein synthesis or cell division, so mature red cells cannot divide and live only about 120 days. Losing the nucleus leaves more room for haemoglobin.

questions.q: Mitochondria are thought to have come from bacteria. One piece of evidence is that new mitochondria:
o: Arise by division of existing mitochondria, much like binary fission
Are made fresh by the Golgi apparatus
Are assembled from parts of the nuclear envelope
Arise from vacuoles in the cytoplasm
questions.x: Mitochondria are never made from scratch; they grow and divide like bacteria. Together with their circular DNA and 70S ribosomes, this supports their bacterial origin.

questions.q: The thickness of the plasma membrane is about:
questions.x: The plasma membrane is roughly 7–10 nm thick, so it can only be resolved with an electron microscope.

questions.q: Very large chromosomes, made of many DNA strands lying side by side, are found in the salivary glands of Drosophila larvae. They are called:
questions.x: Polytene chromosomes form when DNA replicates many times without the cell dividing, so the copies stay together. Lampbrush chromosomes are found in developing egg cells.

questions.q: The receptors of the olfactory epithelium and those of the taste buds belong to the same class because both respond to:
questions.x: Smell and taste receptors are both chemoreceptors: they respond to molecules dissolved in mucus or saliva.

questions.q: In most people, the areas controlling speech and language are found mainly in the:
questions.x: In most people the language areas (for producing and understanding speech) lie in the left cerebral hemisphere. The cerebellum and medulla are not language centres.

questions.q: Colour vision in bright light depends on which photoreceptors?
questions.x: Cones work in bright light and distinguish colours. Rods work in dim light and do not give colour vision.

questions.q: The pia mater is best described as:
o: A tough outer membrane lying next to the skull
A thin, delicate membrane closely attached to the surface of the brain
A layer of white matter beneath the cortex
questions.x: The pia mater is the innermost meninx, thin and rich in blood vessels, following every fold of the brain. The tough outer layer is the dura mater and the web-like middle layer is the arachnoid.

questions.q: The cone-shaped region of the cell body from which the axon arises, where impulses usually start, is the:
questions.x: The axon leaves the cell body at the axon hillock, where action potentials are usually triggered. Nodes of Ranvier are gaps in the myelin further along.

questions.q: Which pairing of a receptor and the form of energy it transduces is correct?
questions.x: Taste cells are chemoreceptors that respond to dissolved chemicals. Cones respond to light, cochlear hair cells to sound vibrations and thermoreceptors to heat.

questions.q: Shedding tears when the eyes are irritated by vapour from a freshly cut onion is an example of:
questions.x: Tear secretion in response to an irritant is inborn and needs no learning, so it is an unconditioned reflex. Conditioned reflexes and habits are acquired through experience.

questions.q: A person keeps holding a hot dish instead of dropping it, overriding the withdrawal reflex. This is possible because:
o: The heat receptors in the skin stop responding
Impulses from the brain can inhibit the motor neurons of the reflex arc
The sensory neuron is disconnected from the spinal cord
The effector muscle loses its nerve supply
questions.x: Descending fibres from the brain synapse on the motor neurons in the spinal cord and can inhibit them, so a reflex can be overridden. The receptors and sensory neurons still work, which is why the heat is felt.

questions.q: Like finding an easier route over a mountain, an enzyme makes a reaction faster by:
o: Providing an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy
Supplying extra energy to the reactants
Raising the temperature of the cell
Increasing the energy released by the reaction
questions.x: The enzyme does not add energy; it offers a pathway with a lower energy barrier, so more molecules can react at body temperature.

questions.q: The hydrolytic enzymes that digest worn-out organelles inside a cell are packed in:
questions.x: Lysosomes are membrane-bound sacs of hydrolytic enzymes used in intracellular digestion. Peroxisomes contain oxidative enzymes such as catalase, not the main digestive hydrolases.

questions.q: Amylase digests starch but cannot digest cellulose, although both are polymers of glucose. This is because:
o: Amylase can only work inside plant cells
The glucose units are joined by different linkages, and only the starch linkage fits amylase's active site
Cellulose molecules are smaller than starch molecules
questions.x: Starch has alpha linkages and cellulose has beta linkages. Amylase's active site fits only the alpha linkage, an example of enzyme specificity.

questions.q: Molecules that bind to an enzyme's allosteric site can:
o: Either increase or decrease the enzyme's activity
questions.x: The allosteric site is a regulatory site. Binding of an inhibitor there lowers activity, while binding of an activator raises it.

questions.q: Which property is shared by enzymes AND inorganic catalysts?
o: Both speed up reactions without being used up
questions.x: All catalysts speed up reactions and are left unchanged. Only enzymes are proteins, are destroyed by heat and show high specificity.

questions.q: Lamarck explained the webbed feet of ducks and other water birds as the result of:
o: Birds with webbed feet surviving better and breeding more
Ancestors stretching their toes while swimming and passing on the change
A sudden mutation in a single duck
Separate creation of each kind of bird
questions.x: Lamarck said water birds spread their toes as they swam, so the skin between them stretched, and this acquired change was inherited. Survival of birds already having webs is Darwin's explanation.

questions.q: Darwin observed that individuals of the same species are not exactly alike. This basic observation is called:
questions.x: Differences among individuals of a species are variations. Natural selection works on these differences.

questions.q: After the ozone layer formed, which major step in the history of life became possible?
o: Living things could move from water onto land
Organic molecules began to form from gases
Lightning first began to strike the Earth
questions.x: Ozone screens out much harmful ultraviolet light. Before it formed, life was safest under water; afterwards organisms could survive on land.

questions.q: In tubal ligation, both oviducts of a woman are cut and tied. This prevents pregnancy because:
o: The uterus can no longer shed its lining
Sperm and oocyte can no longer meet in the oviduct
questions.x: Fertilisation normally happens in the oviduct. With both tubes blocked, sperm cannot reach the oocyte. The ovaries and the cycle continue to work.

questions.q: Shortly after HIV infection, many people have:
o: A short flu-like illness with fever and swollen lymph nodes
Immediate collapse of the immune system
A rash only on the palms and soles
questions.x: The early stage often causes a brief flu-like illness. Years usually pass before the immune system fails and AIDS develops.

questions.q: Normally, how many follicles complete development and release an oocyte in each menstrual cycle?
questions.x: Several follicles begin to grow, but usually only one becomes a mature (Graafian) follicle and ovulates; the rest degenerate.

questions.q: Within an osteon, the lacunae that contain osteocytes are located:
o: Between the concentric lamellae of matrix
questions.x: Osteocytes sit in lacunae lying between the concentric rings (lamellae) of matrix around the Haversian canal. The canals themselves carry blood vessels and nerves.

questions.q: Unlike osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis may also cause:
o: Bony spurs as its main feature
General symptoms such as tiredness and mild fever
Damage limited to one weight-bearing joint
Urate crystals in the joint fluid
questions.x: Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease of the whole body, so it can bring tiredness and fever as well as joint pain. Bony spurs belong to osteoarthritis and urate crystals to gout.

questions.q: In the shoulder joint, the head of the humerus fits into the:
questions.x: The shoulder's socket is the shallow glenoid cavity on the scapula. The acetabulum is the hip socket, and the olecranon is part of the ulna at the elbow.

questions.q: The flexible cartilage that supports the tip of the nose and the walls of the bronchi is:
questions.x: The nose, larynx (mostly), trachea and bronchi are supported by hyaline cartilage. Elastic cartilage is limited to places such as the pinna, epiglottis and Eustachian tube.

questions.q: The sternum consists of three parts. These are the:
questions.x: The sternum (breastbone) has an upper manubrium, a middle body and a lower xiphoid process. Ilium, ischium and pubis form the hip bone.

questions.q: The sliding filament theory of muscle contraction was put forward in 1954 by:
questions.x: Hugh Huxley and Jean Hanson proposed the sliding filament model in 1954 from studies of muscle bands. Watson and Crick described DNA structure, and Schleiden and Schwann the cell theory.

questions.q: Which feature is shared by all three types of muscle?
o: Contraction depends on actin and myosin filaments
questions.x: Smooth, cardiac and skeletal muscle all contract by the interaction of actin and myosin. Smooth muscle lacks striations, only cardiac has intercalated discs, and only skeletal is voluntary.

questions.q: The cytoplasm of a muscle fibre is called the:
questions.x: Sarcoplasm is the cytoplasm of a muscle fibre. The sarcolemma is its cell membrane, a sarcomere is a contractile unit, and axoplasm is the cytoplasm of an axon.

questions.q: Crossing over takes place at the four-strand stage. This means it occurs:
o: Before DNA replication, when each homologue is a single strand
After the homologues have separated in anaphase I
After DNA replication, when each homologue has two chromatids
During the S phase of interphase
questions.x: DNA is replicated in interphase, so in prophase I each bivalent has four chromatids. Crossing over takes place then, between two of these four, and before anaphase I.

questions.q: A human egg is fertilised by a sperm carrying 22 + Y. The zygote will be:
questions.x: The egg always gives 22 + X. Adding 22 + Y gives 44 + XY, which develops as a male.

questions.q: In Drosophila, as in humans, the heterogametic sex is:
questions.x: Drosophila uses the XX–XY system: females are XX and males XY. XO is found in grasshopper males and ZW in female birds.

questions.q: In Mendel's crosses, the offspring produced by crossing two pure-breeding parent plants with contrasting traits form the:
questions.x: The two pure-breeding parents are the P generation and their offspring are the F1. The F2 is obtained only when the F1 plants are self-pollinated.

questions.q: A pure axial-flowered pea plant is crossed with a pure terminal-flowered plant. Axial is dominant. The F1 plants have:
o: Axial and terminal flowers in a 3 : 1 ratio
questions.x: The F1 of two pure lines is all heterozygous, and with complete dominance it shows only the dominant trait, axial flowers. A 3 : 1 ratio appears only in the F2.

questions.q: Which individual produces only one type of gamete?
o: One heterozygous for a single gene
One homozygous for all of its genes
questions.x: Gamete variety comes from heterozygous genes, each giving two possible alleles. An individual homozygous for every gene (for example AABBcc) can make only one kind of gamete.

questions.q: An individual is heterozygous for n genes that assort independently. The number of different gametes it can form is:
questions.x: Each heterozygous gene gives two choices of allele, and the choices are independent, so the gamete types are 2 × 2 × ... = 2ⁿ. For example AaBb (n = 2) gives 4 gametes. 3ⁿ counts genotypes in the offspring of two such parents.

questions.q: An XᴴY father and an XᴴXʰ mother have a first son who is hemophilic. The chance that the next baby is a girl who clots normally is:
questions.x: Every daughter gets the father's Xᴴ, so all daughters clot normally. The chance of a daughter is 1/2, and the earlier son does not change this.

questions.q: Compared with blood in the main artery of the arm, blood in a vein of the arm is:
o: Richer in oxygen and poorer in carbon dioxide
Poorer in oxygen and richer in carbon dioxide
questions.x: The arm tissues take oxygen from the blood and add carbon dioxide, so the returning venous blood has less oxygen. It is under lower pressure and moves towards the heart.

questions.q: The size of an adult human heart is roughly that of a:
o: Clenched fist of the same person
questions.x: The adult heart is about the size of the person's own closed fist. A walnut or bean is far too small, and a football far too large.

questions.q: Which blood vessel is NOT directly connected to the heart?
questions.x: The hepatic portal vein runs from the gut to the liver and never reaches the heart. The aorta, pulmonary trunk and superior vena cava all open into heart chambers.

questions.q: Blood pressure is normally measured on the:
o: Brachial artery of the upper arm
questions.x: The cuff of the sphygmomanometer is wrapped round the upper arm to measure pressure in the brachial artery, which is at about the level of the heart.

questions.q: At rest, the ventricles spend more time in diastole than in systole. This is useful because it:
o: Allows the semilunar valves to stay open longer
Keeps blood pressure in the arteries at zero
Gives the ventricles time to refill and the heart muscle time to rest
Lets the atria and ventricles contract together
questions.x: The long relaxation phase allows the chambers to fill fully and lets the cardiac muscle recover before the next beat, so it does not tire.

questions.q: A newborn mouse has its thymus removed. As it grows, which effect is expected?
o: It cannot make any red blood cells
It has more helper T cells than normal
Few mature T cells form, so cell-mediated immunity is very weak
Its B cells cannot form in the bone marrow
questions.x: T cells mature in the thymus, so without it few functional T cells develop. B cells still arise in the bone marrow, though without helper T cells their antibody response is also poorer.

questions.q: Antibody-mediated immunity is called humoral immunity because the antibodies:
o: Circulate in body fluids such as plasma and lymph
Stay attached to the cells that made them
Are made only in the brain
questions.x: 'Humour' is an old word for body fluid. Antibodies are released into plasma, lymph and other fluids, where they act on antigens.

questions.q: The airways can be divided into a conducting part and a respiratory (gas-exchange) part. Which structures belong to the respiratory part?
o: Respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and alveoli
questions.x: Gas exchange takes place only where there are alveoli: the respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and alveolar sacs. The nose, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi and terminal bronchioles only conduct air.

questions.q: At rest, blood returning from the tissues to the lungs is still about 75% saturated with oxygen. This shows that:
o: The tissues cannot use oxygen from haemoglobin
Most oxygen reaches the tissues dissolved in plasma
The lungs fail to load haemoglobin fully
Only about a quarter of the oxygen carried is given up at rest, leaving a reserve for activity
questions.x: Blood arrives at the tissues about 97% saturated and leaves about 75% saturated, so only roughly a quarter of its oxygen is unloaded at rest. During exercise the low pO₂ in muscles releases much more of this reserve.

questions.q: The scroll-like bony projections (conchae) on the side walls of the nasal cavity help the nose to condition air by:
o: Producing sound when air passes over them
Increasing the area of moist, blood-rich lining over which the air passes
Closing the nasal cavity during swallowing
Absorbing oxygen directly into the blood
questions.x: The conchae make the air swirl over a large surface of moist mucous membrane with many blood vessels, so the air is warmed, moistened and filtered. No gas exchange happens in the nose.

questions.q: Which statement about smoking tobacco through a water pipe (shisha or hookah) is correct?
o: The water removes all harmful substances from the smoke
The smoke still delivers nicotine, carbon monoxide and tar to the lungs
It contains no nicotine and is not addictive
It cannot cause any lung disease
questions.x: Passing the smoke through water cools it but does not remove nicotine, carbon monoxide or tar. A long shisha session can expose the user to large amounts of these substances.

questions.q: Saliva contains an enzyme that helps protect the mouth by attacking the cell walls of bacteria. This enzyme is:
questions.x: Lysozyme in saliva (and tears) breaks down bacterial cell walls. Lipase digests fats, pepsin digests proteins in the stomach, and maltase digests maltose.

questions.q: Which teeth have a single pointed cusp and are used mainly for gripping and tearing food?
questions.x: Canines are the pointed teeth beside the incisors, used to grip and tear food. Incisors cut, while premolars and molars crush and grind.

questions.q: Excess amino acids in the body are deaminated rather than kept because:
o: The body cannot store excess amino acids
Amino acids cannot enter the liver
Amino acids are used only by plants
questions.x: Unlike glucose (stored as glycogen) or fat, surplus amino acids cannot be stored, so their nitrogen is removed and excreted.

questions.q: Taking large amounts of certain painkillers regularly for years can lead to chronic kidney failure because these drugs:
o: Make the bladder muscle contract permanently
Can slowly damage the kidney tissue
Are converted into uric acid stones
Stop the liver from producing urea
questions.x: Long-term overuse of some painkillers gradually injures kidney tissue, a recognised cause of chronic kidney failure.

questions.q: The energy for active reabsorption by the cells of the proximal convoluted tubule is supplied as ATP by their:
questions.x: PCT cells are packed with mitochondria that make ATP by aerobic respiration to power their pumps. Microvilli increase surface area but do not make energy.

questions.q: The raw materials fed into the ornithine cycle to make urea are:
questions.x: Ammonia from deamination and carbon dioxide from respiration are combined in the liver to form urea, CO(NH2)2.

questions.q: Filtrate forms at 120 mL per minute and urine at 1.2 mL per minute. What percentage of the filtrate is reabsorbed?
questions.x: Reabsorbed volume is 120 - 1.2 = 118.8 mL per minute, and 118.8 / 120 = 0.99, so 99% is reabsorbed. 1% is the fraction left as urine, and 98.8 is the wrong result of subtracting without dividing.

questions.q: In sudden cold, the adrenal glands release adrenaline, which helps raise body heat by:
questions.x: Adrenaline speeds up metabolism for a short time, releasing extra heat. Thyroxine has a similar but longer-term effect.

questions.q: P and Q excrete equal amounts of uric acid daily. P passes 1 litre of urine at pH 5; Q passes 2 litres at pH 6.5. Who is at greater risk of uric acid stones, and why?
o: Q, because the urine volume is larger
Q, because the urine is less acidic
Both equally, because the amount of uric acid is the same
P, because the urine is more concentrated and more acidic
questions.x: Uric acid crystallises when urine is concentrated and acidic. P's urine is twice as concentrated and more acidic, so P has the higher risk.

questions.q: Which treatment removes a kidney stone with no cut in the skin, using a thin telescope passed up through the urethra and bladder?
questions.x: In ureteroscopy the instrument goes up the natural urinary passages to reach the stone. Keyhole and open surgery both need a cut.

questions.q: Each renal artery, which brings blood to a kidney, arises directly from the:
questions.x: The renal arteries are branches of the abdominal aorta, so the kidneys receive blood at high pressure. The renal veins drain into the inferior vena cava.

questions.q: Retroviruses have been used as vectors in some gene therapy because they:
o: Insert their genetic material into the host cell's chromosomes
Make proteins without using the host cell
Destroy the faulty gene in the patient
questions.x: A retrovirus makes a DNA copy of its RNA and integrates it into the host's chromosome, so the inserted normal gene is copied each time the cell divides. It adds a working gene rather than destroying the faulty one.

questions.q: The gene inserted in gene therapy for cystic fibrosis codes for:
o: A chloride-ion channel protein (CFTR) in cell membranes
questions.x: Cystic fibrosis is caused by a faulty CFTR gene; the protein is a chloride channel, and its failure produces thick, sticky mucus. Adenosine deaminase is the enzyme missing in one form of SCID.

questions.q: After transformation, bacteria are spread on agar containing an antibiotic. The plasmid carries a resistance gene for that antibiotic. Bacteria that did NOT take up any plasmid will:
o: Fail to grow, because they are killed by the antibiotic
Grow and make the foreign protein
questions.x: Only bacteria carrying the plasmid have the resistance gene, so only they survive on the antibiotic plate. Untransformed bacteria are killed, which allows the transformed ones to be selected.

questions.q: Ethanol burns in air: C₂H₅OH + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O (unbalanced). After balancing, what is the mole ratio of O₂ used to CO₂ formed?
questions.x: Balanced: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O (7 O atoms on each side). So O₂ : CO₂ = 3 : 2. Forgetting the oxygen already in ethanol gives the wrong coefficient for O₂.

questions.q: Method X gives 6 g of a product whose theoretical yield is 8 g. Method Y gives 9 g of the same product from a theoretical yield of 12 g. Which statement is correct?
o: Method Y is more efficient because it gives more product
Method X has the higher percentage yield
Method Y has a percentage yield of 133%
Both methods have the same percentage yield of 75%
questions.x: X: 6/8 × 100 = 75%; Y: 9/12 × 100 = 75%. The larger mass from Y only reflects a larger scale, not a better yield.

questions.q: For 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, equal numbers of moles of magnesium and oxygen are mixed and the magnesium is ignited. Which statement is correct?
o: Oxygen is limiting and half of the magnesium is left over
Neither is limiting, because equal moles were taken
Magnesium is limiting and half of the oxygen is left over
Oxygen is limiting because it is a gas
questions.x: n mol of Mg needs only n/2 mol of O₂, so with n mol of each the magnesium is used up first and n/2 mol of O₂ remains.

questions.q: The total number of lobes in the three 2p orbitals of an atom taken together is:
questions.x: Each p orbital has two lobes, and there are three p orbitals (px, py, pz), giving 3 × 2 = 6 lobes.

questions.q: An electron has n = 3 and l = 1. The shape of the orbital it occupies is:
questions.x: l = 1 is a p orbital (here 3p), which is dumbbell-shaped. l = 0 would be spherical, and l = 2 a d orbital.

questions.q: A node in an orbital is a point, surface or plane where:
o: The probability of finding the electron is greatest
The electron has its highest energy
The probability of finding the electron is zero
Two orbitals of different shells overlap
questions.x: A node is a region of zero electron density. For example, the nucleus lies in the nodal plane of a p orbital.

questions.q: At the same temperature and pressure, 2 dm³ of H₂ and 2 dm³ of CO₂ are taken. The ratio of the mass of H₂ to the mass of CO₂ is: (H 1, C 12, O 16)
questions.x: Equal volumes at the same T and P contain equal numbers of moles, so the mass ratio equals the molar mass ratio: 2 : 44 = 1 : 22.

questions.q: At 1 atm, water freezes at 273 K. On the kelvin scale, it boils at:
questions.x: Water boils at 100 °C, and 100 + 273 = 373 K. A change of 1 °C equals a change of 1 K.

questions.q: Smoke particles in still air, seen under a microscope, move about in an irregular zig-zag way. This observation shows that:
o: They are being hit unevenly by fast-moving air molecules
The smoke particles are attracted to one another
Air molecules are at rest and the particles push them
The smoke particles are themselves gas molecules
questions.x: This Brownian motion is caused by unequal bombardment of the particles by invisible air molecules that are moving rapidly and randomly. It is direct evidence for the motion of gas molecules.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a property of liquids?
o: A definite shape of their own
questions.x: Liquids have a definite volume, flow and diffuse, but take the shape of their container because their molecules can slide past one another.

questions.q: Which pair of compounds is isomorphous, both having a 1 : 1 atomic ratio and the same cubic crystal form?
questions.x: NaF and MgO have the same atomic ratio and the same cubic structure. CaF₂ has a 1 : 2 ratio, and diamond and graphite are two forms of one element.

questions.q: Which of these alkali metal halides has the smallest magnitude of lattice energy?
questions.x: All the ions are singly charged, so the compound with the largest cation and anion (Cs⁺ and I⁻) has the weakest attraction and smallest lattice energy.

questions.q: Extra chlorine gas is pumped into a vessel holding PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g) at equilibrium, keeping volume and temperature fixed. What follows?
o: The equilibrium shifts to the left and more PCl₅ forms
The equilibrium shifts to the right and more PCl₃ forms
questions.x: Adding a product makes the system use some of it up, so the reverse reaction is favoured. Kc does not change at constant temperature.

questions.q: A buffer made from ethanoic acid and sodium ethanoate has a pH that is:
questions.x: A weak acid with its salt forms an acidic buffer; with similar amounts its pH is near the pKa of ethanoic acid, 4.74.

questions.q: The units of Ksp for AgCl are:
questions.x: Ksp = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻] = (mol dm⁻³)(mol dm⁻³) = mol² dm⁻⁶.

questions.q: 0.1 g of magnesium ribbon reacts with excess dilute H₂SO₄. Which change increases BOTH the initial rate and the total volume of hydrogen collected?
o: Using 0.2 g of the same ribbon
questions.x: Magnesium is the limiting reagent, so only more magnesium gives more H₂; twice the ribbon also has twice the surface area, so the rate rises. The other changes speed the reaction but give the same volume.

questions.q: If the reaction H₂ + I₂ → 2HI took place in a single elementary step, the molecularity of that step would be:
questions.x: Molecularity counts the particles colliding in one elementary step: one H₂ and one I₂, so the step is bimolecular.

questions.q: Given: C(s) + O₂ → CO₂, ΔH = −394 kJ; H₂ + ½O₂ → H₂O(l), ΔH = −286 kJ; C₂H₂ + 2½O₂ → 2CO₂ + H₂O(l), ΔH = −1300 kJ. What is ΔHf of ethyne, C₂H₂?
2.1 kJ of heat is supplied to 100 g of water. By how much does its temperature rise? (specific heat capacity of water = 4.2 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹)
questions.x: ΔT = q/(m c) = 2100/(100 × 4.2) = 5 K. Forgetting to change kJ into J would give a far too small rise.

questions.q: Work and energy are sometimes expressed in dm³ atm. One dm³ atm is equal to about:
questions.x: 1 atm = 101 325 Pa and 1 dm³ = 10⁻³ m³, so 1 dm³ atm = 101.3 Pa m³ = 101.3 J. 8.314 and 0.0821 are values of R.

questions.q: When sulphur dioxide is converted into sulphate ion (SO₂ → SO₄²⁻), sulphur is:
questions.x: S in SO₂ is +4 and in SO₄²⁻ is +6; an increase in oxidation number is oxidation.

questions.q: In the reaction 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂, which atoms are reduced?
o: Hydrogen atoms of water, from +1 to 0
Oxygen atoms of water, from −2 to 0
Hydrogen atoms of water, from 0 to +1
questions.x: Some hydrogen falls from +1 in water to 0 in H₂ gas, a reduction; sodium is oxidised and oxygen stays at −2.

questions.q: Bond energies are usually given in the unit:
questions.x: Bond energy is the energy per mole of bonds, so it is expressed in kilojoules per mole. The debye is the unit of dipole moment.

questions.q: Which of the following molecules is linear?
questions.x: In CS₂ the carbon has two double-bond regions and no lone pair, so they lie at 180°. H₂S, SO₂ and OF₂ all have lone pairs on the central atom and are bent.

questions.q: Fluoromethane, CH₃F (M = 34), boils at a higher temperature than ethane, C₂H₆ (M = 30). The main reason is that:
o: CH₃F is polar, so dipole–dipole forces act between its molecules
CH₃F has a much larger molar mass
The C–F bond is broken during boiling
questions.x: The molar masses are similar, so the difference comes from polarity. The polar C–F bond gives CH₃F a dipole, adding dipole–dipole attraction that ethane lacks.

questions.q: Where in the periodic table is an atom with outer electrons 3d⁵ 4s² (argon core) placed?
questions.x: The last electrons fill 3d, so it is d-block; the outermost shell is n = 4 (period 4); 5 + 2 = 7 outer electrons put it in Group VIIB (manganese).

questions.q: The Na⁺ ion is much smaller than the Na atom because:
o: Removing the 3s electron removes the whole outer shell
The nucleus gains protons when the ion forms
The ion has more electrons than the atom
Shielding increases when the electron is lost
questions.x: Na is 2,8,1 and Na⁺ is 2,8; losing the third shell, with the same 11 protons pulling on fewer electrons, makes the ion much smaller.

questions.q: In potassium permanganate, KMnO₄, manganese (Mn: [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s²) is in the +7 state. How many 3d electrons does manganese have in this state?
questions.x: Mn has 7 electrons beyond argon (3d⁵ 4s²). In the +7 state all seven are used, leaving 3d⁰. Five is the number in the neutral atom.

questions.q: The very large number of organic compounds is mainly due to:
o: Carbon being a metal that forms many ions
Carbon having the highest electronegativity of all elements
Organic compounds being made only by living things
Carbon's ability to form chains and rings and multiple bonds, together with isomerism
questions.x: Catenation, single, double and triple bonds, and the many isomers possible for one formula give millions of carbon compounds. Carbon is a non-metal and forms covalent bonds.

questions.q: How many moles of hydrogen are needed to hydrogenate one mole of but-1-en-3-yne, CH₂=CH–C≡CH, completely to butane?
questions.x: The C=C bond needs 1 mol H₂ and the C≡C bond needs 2 mol H₂, a total of 3 mol.

questions.q: In the Friedel–Crafts alkylation of benzene with chloromethane and AlCl₃, the electrophile is:
questions.x: AlCl₃ removes Cl⁻ from CH₃Cl to form AlCl₄⁻ and the methyl carbocation CH₃⁺, which attacks the ring.

questions.q: Free radicals are very reactive because:
o: They have an unpaired electron that tends to pair up by forming a bond
They carry a large positive charge
They have a complete octet of electrons
They are always very heavy species
questions.x: The unpaired electron makes a radical unstable, so it reacts quickly to gain a partner electron. Radicals are neutral and do not have a complete octet.

questions.q: Ethyne is reacted with one mole of hydrogen using Lindlar's catalyst. The product is:
questions.x: Lindlar's catalyst is a poisoned palladium catalyst that stops hydrogenation at the alkene stage.

questions.q: Benzene is converted into cyclohexane by:
o: Shaking with hydrogen at room temperature without a catalyst
Heating with hydrogen in the presence of finely divided nickel
questions.x: Catalytic hydrogenation needs a metal catalyst such as Ni (or Pt, Pd) and heat, because the stable aromatic ring resists addition.

questions.q: Choosing the six-carbon parent chain of CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₃ and numbering it correctly gives the systematic name:
questions.x: The longest chain has six carbons. Numbering from the right end puts the methyl groups on carbons 2 and 4, lower than 3 and 5 from the left.

questions.q: Propan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH, is heated with excess concentrated H₂SO₄. The alkene formed is:
questions.x: Dehydration removes H₂O from the alcohol, leaving a C=C bond in the same three-carbon chain: CH₃CH=CH₂, propene.

questions.q: In dehydrohalogenation of an alkyl halide, the hydrogen atom removed along with the halogen comes from:
o: The α-carbon, which bears the halogen
Any carbon at the far end of the chain
The β-carbon, next to the carbon bearing the halogen
The base used in the reaction
questions.x: The H and X are lost from neighbouring carbons (β-elimination), so a C=C double bond forms between the α- and β-carbons.

questions.q: In which bond does the carbon atom carry the smallest partial positive charge?
questions.x: Iodine is the least electronegative halogen, so the C–I bond is the least polar and its carbon is the least positive. Fluorine, the most electronegative, gives the largest partial charge.

questions.q: Nitration of phenol with dilute nitric acid gives very little of which isomer?
questions.x: The –OH group directs the NO₂ group to the ortho (2-) and para (4-) positions, so the meta isomer, 3-nitrophenol, is formed in only a very small amount.

questions.q: Phenol reacts with metallic sodium to give:
questions.x: 2C₆H₅OH + 2Na → 2C₆H₅ONa + H₂. Water is the by-product only when phenol reacts with NaOH, not with sodium metal.

questions.q: Butanal, CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO, is reduced with NaBH₄. The product is:
questions.x: Reduction of an aldehyde adds two H atoms across the C=O, giving a primary alcohol, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH (butan-1-ol). Butan-2-ol would come from the ketone butanone.

questions.q: The only aldehyde that gives a positive iodoform (triiodomethane) test is:
questions.x: The iodoform test needs a CH₃CO– group. Among aldehydes only ethanal, CH₃CHO, has a methyl group joined to the carbonyl carbon.

questions.q: Ethanoic acid is treated with chlorine in the presence of red phosphorus. The main organic product is:
questions.x: Chlorine replaces an α-hydrogen (on the carbon next to –COOH) to give ClCH₂COOH. Ethanoyl chloride is made with SOCl₂ or PCl₅, not Cl₂.

questions.q: Disulphide (–S–S–) bridges that help hold the shape of many proteins are formed between units of the amino acid:
questions.x: Cysteine has an –SH group in its side chain, and two –SH groups can join to form an –S–S– bridge. Glycine, alanine and lysine contain no sulphur.

questions.q: The linkage that joins the repeating units in a polyester such as Terylene is:
questions.x: A polyester forms when –COOH and –OH groups condense, giving ester links. The amide link –CO–NH– belongs to nylons.

questions.q: Two forces of 10 N each act on a body, one along the positive x-axis and the other at 60° to it. Using rectangular components (cos 60° = 0.5, sin 60° = √3/2), the magnitude of the resultant is:
questions.x: Rx = 10 + 10 cos 60° = 15 N and Ry = 10 sin 60° = 5√3 N. R = √(225 + 75) = √300 = 10√3 N. 20 N would need the forces to be parallel.

questions.q: At the top of its flight, reached 2 s after being launched, a projectile moves at 15 m s⁻¹. What was its speed at launch? (g = 10 m s⁻², no air drag)
questions.x: Horizontal component = 15 m s⁻¹ (the speed at the top). Vertical component at launch = g × 2 = 20 m s⁻¹. Launch speed = √(15² + 20²) = 25 m s⁻¹.

questions.q: A man walks 12 m due east and then 5 m due south. The magnitude of his displacement from the starting point is:
questions.x: The two walks are at right angles, so displacement = √(12² + 5²) = √169 = 13 m. 17 m is the distance, not the displacement.

questions.q: A ball is fired at 40 m s⁻¹ with a 30° launch angle (sin 30° = 0.5). Three seconds into the flight, what is the vertical part of its velocity? Take g = 10 m s⁻² and neglect air drag.
questions.x: Initial vertical component = 40 × 0.5 = 20 m s⁻¹ upward. After 3 s: 20 − 10 × 3 = −10 m s⁻¹, i.e. 10 m s⁻¹ downward; the ball is already falling.

questions.q: A body's displacement over a certain time interval is zero. The distance it travelled in that interval:
o: May be zero or greater than zero
questions.x: Zero displacement means the body ended where it started. It may have stayed at rest (zero distance) or gone away and come back (positive distance). Distance is never negative.

questions.q: Ignoring air resistance, at the highest point of an oblique (angled) projectile's path, its speed is:
questions.x: At the top the vertical component is zero but the horizontal component remains, so the speed is at its minimum value v cos θ, which is not zero.

questions.q: A ball is thrown horizontally at 20 m s⁻¹ from a tall tower. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m s⁻², after 2 s the ratio of its vertical drop to its horizontal distance is:
questions.x: Horizontal distance = 20 × 2 = 40 m. Vertical drop = ½ × 10 × 2² = 20 m. Ratio = 20 : 40 = 1 : 2.

questions.q: A 2 kg body has a linear momentum of 10 kg m s⁻¹. Its kinetic energy is:
questions.x: KE = p²/2m = 100 ÷ 4 = 25 J. Using p²/m gives 50 J, which forgets the factor 2.

questions.q: One watt is equal to:
questions.x: Power is the rate of doing work, so 1 watt is 1 joule of work done per second.

questions.q: A block slides down a fixed smooth inclined plane. The work done on the block by the normal reaction of the plane is:
o: Positive, because the block speeds up
Zero, because the normal force is perpendicular to the displacement
Negative, because the normal force opposes gravity
Equal to the loss of potential energy of the block
questions.x: The normal reaction acts at 90° to the surface, and the block moves along the surface, so cos 90° = 0 and the work is zero. The speeding up is due to gravity.

questions.q: The angular velocity of a wheel rises uniformly from 10 rad s⁻¹ to 30 rad s⁻¹ in 4 s. Its angular acceleration is:
questions.x: Angular acceleration is the rate of change of angular velocity: α = Δω/Δt = (30 − 10)/4 = 5 rad s⁻².

questions.q: A river flows smoothly through a wide section but becomes turbulent where it is forced through a narrow gap between rocks. The best explanation is that in the gap:
o: The water slows down, by continuity, and becomes more viscous
The water's density increases, so it becomes turbulent
The pressure rises sharply, which always makes flow turbulent
The water speeds up, by continuity, and exceeds the critical velocity
questions.x: By continuity (Av = constant) the water moves faster where the area is smaller. Once its speed is above the critical velocity, the flow turns turbulent.

questions.q: When a shower is turned on, the light shower curtain tends to move inward toward the stream of water. This is because:
o: The water makes the curtain heavier
The moving water and air inside the shower are at lower pressure than the still air outside
The air inside the shower is at higher pressure than outside
The curtain is attracted by static charge only
questions.x: Fast-moving air dragged along by the water has lower pressure (Bernoulli's effect), so the higher pressure of the still air outside pushes the curtain in.

questions.q: Two small spheres move through the same viscous liquid under Stokes' law. Their radii are in the ratio 1 : 2 and their speeds in the ratio 3 : 1. The ratio of the drag forces on them is:
questions.x: F ∝ rv, so F₁ : F₂ = (1 × 3) : (2 × 1) = 3 : 2. Squaring the radius would wrongly give 3 : 4.

questions.q: Blood speeds up as it passes through a narrowed section of an artery. According to Bernoulli's principle, the extra kinetic energy of the blood comes from:
o: A fall in the pressure of the blood
A rise in the pressure of the blood
Heat produced by the artery wall
An increase in the blood's density
questions.x: In horizontal flow P + ½ρv² is constant, so a gain in kinetic energy per unit volume is paid for by an equal fall in pressure.

questions.q: The intensity of a wave is defined as:
o: The energy carried per unit time per unit area perpendicular to the direction of travel
The maximum displacement of the particles
The number of waves passing a point per second
questions.x: Intensity is power per unit area, measured in W m⁻². For a given wave it increases with the square of the amplitude.

questions.q: Waves of speed 24 m s⁻¹ and frequency 60 Hz form a stationary wave on a string. The distance between adjacent nodes is:
questions.x: λ = v/f = 24/60 = 0.4 m, and adjacent nodes are λ/2 = 0.2 m apart. 0.4 m is the full wavelength.

questions.q: Three waves overlap at a point. At one instant their displacements there are +4 mm, −1 mm and +2 mm. The resultant displacement is:
questions.x: By the principle of superposition the displacements add with their signs: 4 − 1 + 2 = +5 mm. Ignoring the sign of −1 mm gives +7 mm.

questions.q: Two particles on a rope carrying a progressive transverse wave are half a wavelength apart. When one of them is at a crest, the other is:
o: At its mean position, moving up
At its mean position, moving down
questions.x: Points λ/2 apart vibrate in opposite phase (phase difference π). So when one is at a crest, the other is at a trough.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT carried from place to place by a progressive water wave?
questions.x: A progressive wave carries energy and the disturbance forward, and can carry a signal. The water particles only vibrate about their mean positions; there is no net transport of water.

questions.q: The speed of sound in air calculated from Newton's formula was found to be:
o: About 16% more than the measured value
Exactly equal to the measured value
About 16% less than the measured value
questions.x: Newton's formula gives about 280 m s⁻¹ at STP, while experiment gives about 332 m s⁻¹. The shortfall of roughly 16% was later explained by Laplace.

questions.q: A bullet strikes a wooden block and stops inside it, and both become warm. In terms of energy, this shows that:
o: The kinetic energy of the bullet has become internal energy
Energy has been destroyed in the collision
Heat has been created from nothing
The internal energy of the bullet has become kinetic energy
questions.x: The bullet's kinetic energy is not lost; work done against the wood turns it into internal energy of the bullet and the block, so they warm up.

questions.q: A gas sample occupies 2 litres at 300 K under a steady 1 × 10⁵ Pa. It is warmed to 450 K with the pressure unchanged. How much work does it do on its surroundings? (1 litre = 10⁻³ m³)
questions.x: At constant pressure V ∝ T, so V = 2 × 450/300 = 3 litres. ΔV = 1 × 10⁻³ m³, so W = 1 × 10⁵ × 1 × 10⁻³ = 100 J. Using the final volume gives 300 J.

questions.q: A gas absorbs 100 J of heat and at the same time 50 J of work is done on it by a piston. The change in its internal energy is:
questions.x: Both the heat supplied and the work done on the gas add energy to it: ΔU = 100 + 50 = +150 J.

questions.q: Moving 1 C between two points 1 V apart takes 1 J. How much work is needed to move 1 μC through a potential difference of 1 kV?
questions.x: 1 V = 1 J C⁻¹, so W = qV = 10⁻⁶ C × 10³ V = 10⁻³ J. Getting the prefixes wrong gives the other values.

questions.q: Electric potential and potential difference are both measured in:
questions.x: The volt (J C⁻¹) is the SI unit of both potential and potential difference. N C⁻¹ is a unit of electric field, the ampere of current, the coulomb of charge.

questions.q: An energy of 1 MeV is equal to: (1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J)
questions.x: 1 MeV = 10⁶ eV = 10⁶ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ J. Using 10³ (keV) gives 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁶ J.

questions.q: A battery of emf 12 V gives a terminal potential difference of 10 V while supplying 2 A to a resistor. The resistance of the external resistor is:
questions.x: The external resistor has the terminal p.d. across it: R = V/I = 10 ÷ 2 = 5 Ω. Using the emf gives 6 Ω; 1 Ω is the internal resistance.

questions.q: A charged particle circles at right angles to a uniform magnetic field. Its speed and the flux density are both doubled. Compared with before, its radius and its period are:
questions.x: r = mv/(qB): doubling v and B leaves r the same. T = 2πm/(qB) does not depend on v, so doubling B halves T.

questions.q: A wire lies at right angles to a uniform field. If both the current in it and its length inside the field are doubled, the force on it becomes:
questions.x: F = ILB, so doubling both I and L multiplies the force by 2 × 2 = 4.

questions.q: In the equation ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt, the negative sign represents:
questions.x: The minus sign shows that the induced emf opposes the change in flux that produces it, which is Lenz's law.

questions.q: An alternating voltage is given by v = 100 sin(100πt) volts. Its frequency is:
questions.x: Compare with v = V₀ sin ωt: ω = 100π rad s⁻¹ = 2πf, so f = 100π/2π = 50 Hz.

questions.q: In a half-wave rectifier with an ideal diode, what is the voltage across the load resistor during the half-cycle in which the diode is reverse biased?
o: Equal to the peak input voltage
Equal to the peak input voltage but reversed
questions.x: A reverse-biased ideal diode is an open circuit, so no current flows through the load and the voltage across it is zero for that half-cycle.

questions.q: The wave theory of light fails to explain the photoelectric effect because it predicts that:
o: Electrons should be emitted only above a threshold frequency
The maximum kinetic energy should rise with frequency
Light of any frequency should eject electrons if it is intense enough
questions.x: On the wave picture, energy depends on intensity, so even low-frequency light should work if bright enough. Experiments show a threshold frequency, which the photon model explains.

questions.q: A hydrogen electron is in the n = 2 level, of energy −3.4 eV. The minimum energy needed to free it from the atom is:
questions.x: To free the electron its energy must be raised to zero, so it needs 0 − (−3.4) = 3.4 eV. 13.6 eV applies only to an electron in the ground state.

questions.q: Polonium-210 (²¹⁰₈₄Po) undergoes alpha decay. The daughter nucleus is:
questions.x: An alpha particle carries away A = 4 and Z = 2: 210 − 4 = 206, 84 − 2 = 82, which is lead-206.

questions.q: During its book fair week, a bookshop gives 20 per cent off any book priced above 500 rupees and 10 per cent off every other book. Bags are free, but gift-wrapping costs 50 rupees a book. Sara buys a dictionary priced at 800 rupees and two story books priced at 300 rupees each, and asks for only the dictionary to be gift-wrapped. According to the passage, how much does Sara pay in all?
questions.x: Dictionary: 800 less 20% = 640. Story books: 300 less 10% = 270 each, so 540. Adding 50 rupees for wrapping one book gives 640 + 540 + 50 = 1,230 rupees.

questions.q: "Hope is a lamp the traveller keeps, / Burning low while the desert sleeps." What does the poet suggest about hope?
o: It is dangerous, like fire in a dry desert
It goes out completely when night comes
It belongs only to people who travel
It gives quiet guidance and comfort in hard times
questions.x: The metaphor compares hope to a lamp that keeps burning in the dark, lonely desert, so hope guides and comforts in hard times. The lamp keeps burning, so it does not go out at night.

questions.q: In "The players and their coach celebrated the win, and then they all went out for dinner", the antecedent of 'they' is:
questions.x: 'They' is plural and 'all' shows it covers everyone mentioned, so it refers to the compound antecedent 'the players and their coach'.

questions.q: Choose the word that best fits: "Ayesha ___ at the beautiful painting for several minutes, unable to look away."
questions.x: To 'gaze' is to look steadily for a long time; 'glanced' and 'glimpsed' describe very brief looks, which clash with 'several minutes'.

questions.q: Choose the correct preposition: "Please submit your admission form ___ Friday at the latest."
questions.x: 'By' with a time means 'not later than', which fits a deadline.

questions.q: How should 'however' be punctuated when it joins two complete clauses?
o: I wanted to go out, however it was raining.
I wanted to go out however, it was raining.
I wanted to go out; however it was raining,
I wanted to go out; however, it was raining.
questions.x: When 'however' links two main clauses, a semicolon goes before it and a comma after it.

questions.q: Choose the correct form: "Ayesha finished ___ the report just before the deadline."
questions.x: 'Finish' is followed by a gerund, not an infinitive.

questions.q: Choose the correct preposition: "The frightened kitten is hiding ___ the bed."
questions.x: 'Under' is a preposition of position meaning below; the others are prepositions of time.

questions.q: Choose the correct word: "After the operation, the patient is recovering ____."
questions.x: An adverb is needed to describe how the patient is recovering. 'Well' is the adverb; 'good' is an adjective and 'goodness' is a noun.

questions.q: In a town, 80% of road accidents involve cars driven by men. Someone concludes that men are worse drivers than women. Which missing fact is most needed before this conclusion can be judged?
o: How many hospitals there are in the town
What share of the cars on the town's roads are driven by men
The average price of a car in the town
How many accidents happened in the previous year
questions.x: If men drive about 80% of the cars, 80% of accidents is exactly what we would expect. Without the share of drivers, the figure says nothing about skill.

questions.q: A coin is suspected of being unfair. Which result gives the best reason to believe that it is fair?
o: In 4 tosses it landed heads 3 times
It looks the same on both sides
In 1000 tosses it landed heads 497 times
The shopkeeper said it was a normal coin
questions.x: A large number of tosses landing heads close to half the time is real evidence of fairness. Four tosses are far too few, and looks or someone's word are not tests.

questions.q: Find the next pair: CX, EV, GT, ?
questions.x: The first letters go C, E, G, I (+2) and the second letters go X, V, T, R (-2), giving IR.

questions.q: Find the next number: 2, 4, 7, 12, 19, 30, ?
questions.x: The differences are the prime numbers 2, 3, 5, 7, 11. The next prime is 13, so 30 + 13 = 43.

questions.q: Adeel, Babar, Danish, Ehsan, Farhan and Gohar sit equally spaced around a round table, facing the centre. Adeel sits opposite Ehsan. Babar sits immediately to Adeel's left. Gohar sits opposite Babar. Danish does not sit next to Ehsan. Who sits opposite Danish?
questions.x: Fixing Adeel, Ehsan, Babar and Gohar leaves two seats: one beside Ehsan and one beside Adeel. Danish must take the seat beside Adeel, and the seat opposite it is Farhan's.

questions.q: Box P is heavier than box Q. Box R is lighter than box Q. Which of the three boxes is the heaviest?
questions.x: P is heavier than Q, and Q is heavier than R, so P is the heaviest.

questions.q: Statement: A college's science laboratories stand unused because it has no laboratory assistants. Courses of action: I. The laboratories should be turned into storerooms. II. Laboratory assistants should be hired. Which course(s) of action follow?
questions.x: Hiring assistants solves the stated cause and lets students do practicals again. Turning labs into storerooms gives up on practical work.

questions.q: Statement: Ayesha has an important exam in two days but has developed a high fever. Courses of action: I. She should see a doctor. II. She should stay up all night studying despite the fever. Which course(s) of action follow?
questions.x: A high fever needs medical attention, and recovering will help her sit the exam. Staying up all night while ill would make her worse.

questions.q: Hamza believes that if someone sneezes as he leaves the house, his journey will go badly. Which is a valid reason to reject this belief?
o: People sneeze more often in spring
Hamza does not travel very often
A sneeze is a body reflex to irritation in the nose and cannot affect events on a journey
Sneezing is more common in crowded places
questions.x: A sneeze has a physical cause inside the body. Nothing links it to what happens later on a journey.
